fm01_gaikuang.note: Wenshi ziliao xuanji, the serial publication of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference's historical-materials committee, begun in 1960. It solicited first-person accounts from former Nationalist officials, officers and businessmen — many of them, like Shen Zui, recently pardoned prisoners. Almost the whole of this book first appeared there. The series is indispensable and partisan at once: it preserves testimony that exists nowhere else, and it was commissioned, edited and published by the state the witnesses had fought against, in a period when the value of a memoir was measured partly by how thoroughly its author condemned his former self.

Wen Qiang (1907–2001), Shen Zui's colleague in the Juntong and later a Nationalist lieutenant general; captured at the Huai-Hai campaign in 1949, held as a war criminal and pardoned in 1975, the last group released. He was a distant cousin of Mao Zedong on his mother's side. The word "Comrade" here is doing real work: by the time Shen Zui wrote, Wen Qiang had been rehabilitated into the same CPPCC apparatus that published them both.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: the Fuxingshe, which some people also called the Blue Shirts
fm01_gaikuang.note: The tangle of names is real and is not the author's confusion. Chinese Renaissance Society (中华复兴社), Vigorous Practice Society (力行社) and Blue Shirts (蓝衣社) were used for overlapping bodies in a concentric structure built around Chiang Kai-shek by Whampoa graduates from 1932. "Blue Shirts" was largely an outsiders' and journalists' name — it circulated widely in the foreign press of the 1930s, which cast the group as China's fascists — and members themselves rarely used it. Historians have argued since the 1980s about how much of the "Blue Shirt" organization existed as described and how much was inferred from hostile reporting; Shen Zui's casual "some people also called it" is closer to the truth than most contemporary accounts.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: Inside the Juntong it was known as the Ten-Man Team.
fm01_gaikuang.note: The founding group of Dai Li's service. Rosters differ between accounts, and even the count is not stable — the phrase means "the original ten" rather than a fixed list, and different memoirists name different men among them. Shen Zui joined later and is reporting the service's own founding legend, which by his day was commemorated annually.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: He Zhonghan, Feng Ti, Teng Jie, Zhou Fu, Kang Ze, Gui Yongqing, Pan Youqiang, Zheng Jiemin and Qiu Kaiji
fm01_gaikuang.note: The Lixingshe's founding council, drawn almost entirely from the Whampoa Military Academy's first class. He Zhonghan and Teng Jie were the principal organizers; Kang Ze ran the propaganda side and the Farmer's Bank militia; Gui Yongqing became a senior field commander. Feng Ti was executed in 1938 for the burning of Changsha, the scorched-earth fire set on a false alarm that destroyed the city and killed thousands — one of the war's worst self-inflicted disasters, for which three officials were shot. That Dai Li appears here only as an alternate member is the point of the paragraph: at the founding he was junior to all of these men, and outlasted nearly all of them.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: The department was established on 1 April 1932.
fm01_gaikuang.note: The date is well attested and the service kept it as its birthday for the rest of its existence — see the "April the First Assembly" below. The Juntong dated itself from the founding of this secret-service department of a semi-secret society, not from the bureau whose name it later carried.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: the boss of the CC clique, Chen Lifu
fm01_gaikuang.note: Chen Lifu (1900–2001) and his brother Chen Guofu ran the Kuomintang's party organization and its party-based intelligence service; "CC" is usually explained as the brothers' initials or as "Central Club." The rivalry sketched in this paragraph — party intelligence under the Chens against military intelligence under Dai Li — structures the whole of Nationalist secret-service history, and the 1938 split into Zhongtong and Juntong described further down is its formal settlement.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: his Whampoa class was a late one — the sixth
fm01_gaikuang.note: The Whampoa Military Academy's intake number functioned as a rank of seniority in its own right throughout the Nationalist officer corps, independent of actual position. Dai Li entered with the sixth class in 1926, years behind the first-class men who founded the Lixingshe, and never lost the handicap; the workaround Shen Zui describes — real power as deputy director, the directorship left to a succession of senior figures who did not exercise it — is the standard account of how it was managed.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: the Special Political Problems Research Office, run by Zhang Guotao
fm01_gaikuang.note: Zhang Guotao (1897–1979) was a founder of the Chinese Communist Party, present at its first congress in 1921, and commander of the Fourth Front Army; he lost his power struggle with Mao Zedong on the Long March and defected to the Nationalists in April 1938. The Juntong then put him to work against his former party. Nothing else in this chapter's list of offices carries the weight this half-sentence does, and Shen Zui passes over it without comment — a founder of the Communist Party is a line item between a research office and a recreation room. Zhang Guotao later left for Hong Kong and died in Canada. The scan is unambiguous here; the OCR read the name as a nonentity, and it was crop-verified against the page.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: a Zhongshan Room in charge of recreation
fm01_gaikuang.note: Named for Sun Yat-sen (Sun Zhongshan). Nationalist units maintained a "Zhongshan Room" as a combined reading room, recreation room and political-instruction space — the Nationalist counterpart to the club rooms of other twentieth-century party-armies.

fm01_gaikuang.anchor: the aircraft Dai Li was travelling in flew into Dai Hill
fm01_gaikuang.note: Dai Li died on 17 March 1946 when his aircraft, flying from Qingdao to Nanking in bad weather, struck high ground near Banqiao, south-east of the city. The hill is usually given in Chinese sources as 岱山 Dai Hill or the site as Kunyugou; this book prints 戴山, which is the author's own surname-character for Dai Li himself. The homophone has fed a long afterlife of stories about the coincidence of the name. His death is the hinge of the second half of this book: everything about the Bureau of Secrets Preservation, Zheng Jiemin and Mao Renfeng follows from it.

臭招牌, literally "stinking shop-sign." The idiom is ordinary Chinese for a discredited brand, but the register here is not neutral, and it recurs throughout the book: Shen Zui is writing in the early 1960s, as a pardoned war criminal, for a state publication, about an organization he served in for eighteen years. Where the English keeps expressions like this one, or "criminal activities" and "the reactionaries" below, it is preserving evidence of the conditions the book was written under rather than importing a judgement of its own.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: the first thing I did was to confess my guilt to him
fm02_qianyan.note: 请罪, literally "to beg punishment." Shen Zui had been captured in Yunnan in 1949 and held for eleven years; he was released in the first special amnesty of December 1959, which freed thirty-three war criminals judged to have reformed. The reception described here comes fourteen months later. The confession-first reflex is not a literary flourish: it is the trained posture of a man whose release was conditional on having demonstrated exactly that reflex, and it shapes the whole book.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: Vice-Premiers Chen Yi and Luo Ruiqing
fm02_qianyan.note: Chen Yi (1901–1972), marshal, foreign minister and one of the Communist commanders in the very campaigns that ended Shen Zui's career. Luo Ruiqing (1906–1978) was Minister of Public Security from 1949 to 1959 and by 1961 chief of the general staff: that is, the man who had run the apparatus that held Shen Zui was now in the room receiving him. Neither point is made in the text, and both would be obvious to the book's Chinese readers.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: we had merely served as his unpaid escort
fm02_qianyan.note: 义务随从. The joke lands harder in Chinese, where 义务 means "voluntary, unpaid" in the specific sense used of public-spirited service — Zhou is saying the Juntong's surveillance amounted to a free bodyguard detail. This is the anecdote's governing tone: the Premier is not accusing the man in front of him, he is telling him he was never any good at his job.

The Sun Ya on Nanking Road, opened in 1927, one of the best-known Cantonese establishments in the city and a normal place for a well-dressed man to be seen. Zhou Enlai ran the Communist Party's underground apparatus in Shanghai in the late 1920s and early 1930s, when discovery meant death; the point of the story is that concealment worked best in the most public place available.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: you will have served those who come after as a teacher by negative example
fm02_qianyan.note: 反面教员, "negative-example teacher," a term of art in Chinese political language of the period: a person or thing whose bad example instructs. It was applied to former enemies, to purged officials, and eventually to almost anyone. Here it is the precise job description Zhou Enlai is offering, and it is the commission under which this entire book was written. Every page that follows is shaped by it.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: counts as a further confession, and the government will certainly not call you to account for it
fm02_qianyan.note: The assurance is the hinge of the book's reliability, and it cuts both ways. It removes the strongest reason to conceal — but it also creates an incentive to over-confess, since the value of the testimony to those commissioning it rises with how damning it is. Both pressures should be kept in mind at every point where Shen Zui reports his own crimes.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: what is asked of you is truth, not completeness
fm02_qianyan.note: 要求真实，不求全面. Chen Yi's formula is the editorial charter of the whole Selected Historical Materials project, and it is a genuinely good one for memoir evidence: it asks the witness for what he actually knows rather than for a coherent account, and it explicitly forbids filling gaps. What follows immediately — Chen Yi striking out material that magnified his own part — shows the other edge of the same policy.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: so he had struck all of it out
fm02_qianyan.note: Worth pausing on. In the same breath in which he demands truth and forbids invention, Chen Yi describes deleting accounts of his own guerrilla campaigns because they credited him too much and the Party too little. The standard being set is not simply accuracy; it is accuracy within a frame that requires collective rather than individual agency. That frame operates throughout this book too.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: the seventh day of the lunar year
fm02_qianyan.note: 21 February 1961 was indeed the seventh day of the first lunar month, which is a small but real check on the date: the two calendars agree. The seventh day, 人日 or "Humans' Day," is traditionally the birthday of humankind. Nothing in the text makes anything of that, but it is why the countryside was still keeping the festival.

奉谕速办. This is the sharpest documentary observation in the book, and it is the observation of a man who had the files in his hands. 谕 is the word for a superior's directive and, historically, for an imperial edict; 奉谕 says an order has been received without saying from whom. Shen Zui's point is that the Juntong's killing orders were papered in a formula that recorded authority while naming nobody, so that the archive proves an instruction existed and can never show whose it was. It is a claim about deniability by design, made from the inside, and it is checkable in principle against surviving Nationalist files.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: more than a hundred martyrs were cruelly put to death
fm02_qianyan.note: The Chungking massacre of 27 November 1949, at the Zhazidong and Baigongguan prisons on the eve of the city's fall, in which political prisoners were machine-gunned and the buildings burned. The dead are usually numbered in the low hundreds; the prisons were part of the compound the Sino-American Cooperative Organization had used, which is why the massacre and SACO are permanently linked in Chinese memory. Shen Zui devotes a later chapter to that organization.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: "Child, you may go without office, but you must be a decent human being."
fm02_qianyan.note: 你可以不做官，但要做人. The force of the line is in 做人 — literally "to be/act as a person," meaning to conduct oneself as a human being ought — set against 做官, "to be an official." The pairing makes office and decency alternatives rather than companions. The same phrase supplies the title of the 1980 People's Daily interview reprinted at the end of this book, where Shen Zui says he only learned what 做人 meant after 1949; the preface and the closing piece are bound together by it.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: I have left out the names of some of them, clearly as I remember those names
fm02_qianyan.note: An editorial decision worth noticing, because it is the one place in the preface where Shen Zui says outright that he is withholding something he knows. His stated reason is to protect the relatives; the effect is that the book's account of defectors from the Communist Party is deliberately incomplete in exactly the respect readers would most want to check.

fm02_qianyan.anchor: In 1975, when Zheng Xilin came to Peking on a study visit
fm02_qianyan.note: 1975 is when the last group of imprisoned Nationalist personnel was pardoned, and the "study visits" to Peking were part of that programme. So the verification Shen Zui describes — checking the founding roster with two surviving members of the original group — was possible only because both men had outlived the service, the civil war and twenty-five years of captivity or obscurity. It is also the best evidence in the book of his working method: he checked what he could, with the few people alive who could check it.

ch01.anchor: using resistance to Japan as the pretext, he began energetically preparing for work whose muzzles pointed inward
ch01.note: 枪口对内, "muzzles pointed inward" -- turning the guns on one's own people rather than the invader. The phrase was a standing Communist accusation against the Nationalists in these years, and Shen Zui uses it here of his own service without comment. It is the book's characteristic move: the vocabulary of the accusation has become the vocabulary of the confession.

ch01.anchor: After fighting broke out in Shanghai on 13 August
ch01.note: The Battle of Shanghai, which began on 13 August 1937 and ran three months. It was the largest engagement of the war to that point; Chinese losses were enormous, Shanghai fell in November and Nanking in December. The dates in this paragraph are correct and the sequence -- the plan for a Shanghai or Nanking class overtaken by the speed of the collapse -- matches the record.

ch01.anchor: Every one of these key men was a Communist renegade who had studied in the Soviet Union.
ch01.note: Not a rhetorical flourish. Yu Lexing had been a work-study student in France and then in Moscow; several of the others followed the same route through the Chinese Communist Party's Soviet training in the 1920s before changing sides. Their value to Dai Li was precisely their knowledge of the organization they were now to be used against, and the chapter returns to it later, where renegades teach the course on penetrating Communist organizations and find the work "full of contradiction and very painful."

ch01.anchor: this Trotskyite bandit
ch01.note: 托派匪徒. Liang Ganqiao was a Whampoa first-class graduate who had studied in Moscow and been expelled from the Chinese Communist Party in the Trotskyist purge of 1929 before joining Dai Li's service. In the political language of the period "Trotskyite" had become an all-purpose term of abuse largely detached from Trotsky's politics, and by the 1960s, when Shen Zui was writing, it was among the heaviest labels available. He applies it in passing, as a fact rather than a judgement.

ch01.anchor: more than eleven hundred
ch01.note: The class's size is given three ways in this chapter -- more than eleven hundred at the opening, about seven hundred left by graduation, and "about a thousand" as the number of agents it produced -- and the differences are accounted for in the text by early postings, desertions and withdrawals. The figures are internally consistent, which is worth noting in a memoir written from memory twenty-four years later.

ch01.anchor: Hu Zongnan
ch01.note: Hu Zongnan (1896-1962), Whampoa first class, Chiang Kai-shek's most favoured field commander and from 1937 the dominant military figure in the north-west. He appears throughout this book as a rival power centre to the Juntong; a later chapter is devoted to his dealings with Dai Li and Mao Renfeng. His transfer of sixty women cadets here, against their wishes, is characteristic of how the two organizations traded people.

ch01.anchor: the Central Military Academy's Seventh Branch
ch01.note: The Whampoa academy, renamed the Central Military Academy after 1928, ran numbered branch schools during the war. The Seventh Branch, at Xi'an, was Hu Zongnan's. The women recruited for it had volunteered to fight Japan, which is exactly the objection they raise a few pages later on discovering what the Linli class actually was.

ch01.anchor: the Binli Alumni Association
ch01.note: 滨澧同学会, "the association of those from the banks of the Li" -- the Li being the river at Linli. Shen Zui's chairmanship of it, described at length later in this chapter, is one of the clearest passages in the book about how patronage actually worked inside the Juntong: he funded the association out of Juntong property he was liquidating, and traded placements for the goodwill of the men who controlled the service.

ch01.anchor: the Yunong Embankment
ch01.note: 雨农堤. Yunong, "rain farmer," was Dai Li's style-name, the literary alternative name a Chinese man of his generation used alongside his given name. Naming a walk in the grounds after the absent director is the kind of courtship the chapter is full of; it did Yu Lexing no good at all in the end.

ch01.anchor: a director's office was set up all the same, with Ding Ruoping appointed as its secretary, as a check on the deputy director
ch01.note: The structural point of the whole chapter in one sentence. Dai Li never worked at the class, yet maintained an office there whose function was to watch the man who did. The same design recurs at every level of the organization described in this book, and Shen Zui states it without any suggestion that it was unusual.

ch01.anchor: the head of political training, Wang Zuhua
ch01.note: The political training office is the ideological apparatus of the class, and its head is described here in one breath as an anti-Communist propagandist, the man responsible for "pumping in fascist doctrine," and the officer who vetted the students' opinions. The three functions were not distinguished in practice, which is the point.

ch01.anchor: This woman agent was famous for her ferocity, and even her husband, Xu Yuyi, had been on the receiving end of her pistol.
ch01.note: One of a handful of moments where the roster breaks into anecdote. The Juntong recruited women in numbers and used them for work its men could not do -- surveillance in hotels and households, the "working wives" described below -- and the book's women agents are drawn with the same flat matter-of-factness as its men.

ch01.anchor: Fan Xuewen, Jiang Zhennan, Feng Wenyao and Wang Weizhou
ch01.note: Four men "just back from studying secret-service work in Germany and Italy." Nationalist China sent officers to both fascist states through the 1930s, and Germany supplied China's most important military mission until it was withdrawn in 1938 under Japanese pressure. Jiang Zhennan reappears a few pages later as the author of the class song, adapted from a Nazi party anthem. Jiang Zhennan's name was crop-verified: the OCR gave two different wrong readings of it on the same page.

ch01.anchor: Jin Minjie, a Korean
ch01.note: Koreans in Chinese service were common in this period: after Japan's annexation of Korea in 1910 a large exile community formed in China, and the Korean independence movement worked closely with both Nationalists and Communists. Jin Minjie teaches unarmed combat here, kills a student in a training bout later in the chapter, and is promoted to deputy director of the Juntong's combat class.

ch01.anchor: whichever one they fancied as a "working wife."
ch01.note: 工作太太. The term is the organization's own, and the arrangement it names -- a woman assigned to an agent going into occupied territory, to make his cover plausible and to serve as his household -- was routine. Shen Zui reports it in the same register as the issue of clothing allowances. Nothing in the text suggests the women were consulted.

ch01.anchor: the party anthem of the German fascists
ch01.note: The Horst-Wessel-Lied, the Nazi Party's anthem and from 1933 effectively a second German national anthem. That the Juntong's own song began as an adaptation of it, produced by an instructor fresh from training in Germany, is Shen Zui's joke and also his evidence. The claim is uncorroborated outside this account and is difficult to test, since the surviving Chinese words are not a translation of the German.

ch01.anchor: "safeguard the security of our leader, defend the territory and sovereignty of the state"
ch01.note: 维护我们领袖的安全，保卫国家领土和主权. Shen Zui's point is the order of the two clauses, and Dai Li's pleasure in them. In a song adopted in the second year of a war of national survival, the leader's personal safety comes first and the country's territory second. That is the argument of the passage, and it is made simply by quoting.

ch01.anchor: *Appendix: the words of the class song.
ch01.note: TRANSLATOR'S NOTE. The book prints the full lyric at this point. It is characterised here rather than set out line by line; the two lines that carry Shen Zui's argument are quoted in the paragraph above, where he makes it. Nothing in the argument depends on the remaining text, which is conventional period exhortation. The Chinese is on printed page 20 of the third edition for anyone who wants it.

ch01.anchor: they had thrown down the pen and taken up arms in order to fight Japan, and they had no wish to be secret agents
ch01.note: 投笔从戎, "to throw down the writing-brush and join the army," from the biography of the Han general Ban Chao, who abandoned a copyist's desk for the frontier. The phrase carries real weight in this sentence: these were students who had volunteered out of patriotism and found themselves conscripted into political police work. Of the whole chapter this is the one moment where the people being trained get to state their own position.

ch01.anchor: swearing collectively to join the Juntong
ch01.note: The device is the chapter's most quietly chilling passage, and Shen Zui explains the reasoning himself two paragraphs later: get the formalities of membership done before the students learn what the work is, and "with the chain already round their necks, they could be dealt with." It became standard practice at every subsequent Juntong class.

ch01.anchor: the great victory at Pingxingguan
ch01.note: The engagement of 25 September 1937 in north-eastern Shanxi, in which the Communist Eighth Route Army's 115th Division ambushed a Japanese supply column and destroyed it. Militarily it was a small action; politically it was enormous, the first clear Chinese victory of the war and proof that the Communists were fighting. That is precisely why the class's political officer had to explain it away, and why the students' response -- so even a battle the Communist army wins is a fake -- was so hard to answer.

ch01.anchor: the *New China Daily*
ch01.note: 新华日报, the Chinese Communist Party's newspaper, published legally in Nationalist territory from Hankow in 1938 and then in Chungking until 1947 under the terms of the United Front. Its legality is what makes this passage possible: the students were reading a paper the government permitted, and the class treated possession of it as grounds for secret surveillance.

ch01.anchor: the Lu Xun Academy of Arts in Yan'an
ch01.note: 鲁迅艺术学院, founded in Yan'an in April 1938, the Communist base area's school for writers, artists and musicians. That students at Linli had friends and classmates there, writing to urge them to get out, places the two institutions in the same generation of Chinese young people, sorted by little more than which recruiter reached them first.

ch01.anchor: the agents built a detention room at the class headquarters
ch01.note: TRANSLATION NOTE: 禁闭室, a military detention cell rather than a prison. The OCR read the second character as 财 throughout this passage, which is meaningless here; the reading is from context and is not in doubt.

ch01.anchor: the excellence of the application lies in the mind of the one who applies it
ch01.note: 运用之妙，存乎一心, from the biography of Yue Fei in the History of the Song, where the general answers a question about battle formations by saying that the formation is only the beginning and everything depends on the commander's judgement. It is one of the most famous lines in Chinese military writing. Shen Zui's gloss on what it was taken to mean in the Juntong -- stick at nothing, take no account of any law -- is his own, and the deflation is deliberate.

ch01.anchor: a demolition instructor named Cai
ch01.note: The book gives only the surname. Where a name is incomplete or redacted in the source it is left so here rather than filled in; the redactions later in this chapter, printed as XX in the Chinese, are the author's own or his editors'.

ch01.anchor: Bringing a man down from the third or fourth floor, for example, raises the nice question of whether the operations agent should go in front or behind
ch01.note: This paragraph and the two that follow are the closest thing in the book to a technical manual, and they are the reason it was written. The Juntong's arrest methods were taught orally and never printed -- Shen Zui says so explicitly below -- so a participant's recollection is close to the only source there is. Read as evidence, the passage is unusually credible: it is specific, it is unflattering to the author, and it contains the sort of practical detail nobody inventing an account would think to supply.

ch01.anchor: the cat weeping for the mouse
ch01.note: 猫哭老鼠, the exact Chinese equivalent of crocodile tears -- the cat mourns the mouse it has eaten. Shen Zui applies it to the memorial meeting held for a student the instructors had beaten to death, and the reader should notice that the author was one of the two instructors who beat him.

ch01.anchor: I gave him a heavy blow of the same kind. After these two occasions Yan Xie was so badly injured that he could not be saved
ch01.note: The most direct admission of personal killing in this chapter, made in a single sentence and not returned to. Under the terms of the commission described in the preface, admissions of this kind were what the book existed to produce; that does not make this one less likely to be true, and its very flatness is characteristic. The student's name was crop-verified: the OCR read it two different ways, neither correct.

ch01.anchor: A few drops of croton oil on a piece of beef
ch01.note: 巴豆油, pressed from the seed of Croton tiglium, a violent purgative used in Chinese medicine in minute doses. The book's claim that it kills a dog within half an hour but does a man little harm reflects what was taught at the class rather than pharmacology; croton oil is dangerous to humans in quantity.

ch01.anchor: he was hauled in to serve as "practice material."
ch01.note: 实习品, literally "practice article" -- the word for a specimen or a training aid, applied to a man. The whole episode, in which a doctor suspected of petty embezzlement is publicly tortured through every method the curriculum taught and released without evidence, is offered by Shen Zui as an explanation of what the students learned from it: that the organization stood outside the law entirely.

ch01.anchor: Ye Jianying
ch01.note: Ye Jianying (1897-1986), then Communist chief of staff in the Nationalist-Communist United Front and later one of the People's Republic's marshals. He did teach guerrilla warfare at the Nanyue guerrilla cadre training class in Hunan in early 1939, a genuinely joint Nationalist-Communist institution. Dai Li's response -- planting two of his officers on the course to steal the method for use against its teachers -- is the United Front in miniature.

ch01.anchor: theft is not in itself a capital offence, but as he had failed in his task and shamed Dai Li into the bargain, Dai Li in a rage had him brought back and shot
ch01.note: A summary execution of one of his own battalion commanders, reported in a subordinate clause. The passage is one of several in the book where the scale of Dai Li's personal authority is conveyed not by assertion but by what the narrative treats as unremarkable.

ch01.anchor: a sentry every three paces and a picket every five
ch01.note: 三步一岗，五步一哨, a set phrase for a place under heavy guard. The reception it describes went badly wrong: Dai Li read the display as a warlord's, and his objection -- that if Chiang Kai-shek heard of him putting on airs like this, where would it end -- says a good deal about how precarious the position of even the most feared man in the service was.

ch01.anchor: a Henanese woman student, Liu Ying, who had never been in the water in her life, was drowned
ch01.note: Two deaths are recorded at this class, both in training: this drowning and the beating of Yan Xie. Both surface only because a political instructor used them as ammunition against his superiors at a staff meeting, which is a fair indication of how such things were normally handled.

ch01.anchor: Tang Shengming, then garrison commander there, together with his wife Xu Lai
ch01.note: Tang Shengming (1906-1987) was the younger brother of the general Tang Shengzhi and later went over to the Japanese-sponsored Nanking government at Dai Li's direction, as a planted agent -- one of the more remarkable arrangements of the war. Xu Lai (1909-1973) was among the best-known film actresses of 1930s Shanghai before her marriage. Their appearance here as weekend guests at a graduation ceremony is a fair sample of the world the Juntong moved in.

ch01.anchor: they wept as though for their own parents
ch01.note: 如丧考妣, "as though mourning father and mother," a set phrase that is almost always sardonic in modern usage. Shen Zui is describing his own students, and himself among their patrons, at the moment their protector died.

ch01.anchor: nothing that was not Li was proper and nothing that was not Li would be used
ch01.note: 非澧不视，非澧不用 -- a pun that cannot survive into English. 澧, the Li of Linli, is a homophone of 礼, ritual propriety, and the phrase parodies a famous passage of the Analects in which Confucius tells Yan Hui to look at nothing improper and do nothing improper. The old agents' complaint is thus that promotion now depends not on propriety but on having been at Linli. The English keeps the shape and loses the joke, which is why it is glossed here.

ch01.anchor: instead of "comrade" they said "fellow student,"
ch01.note: 同学 against 同志. "Comrade" was the Juntong's own internal form of address, borrowed like much of its vocabulary from the movement it existed to destroy; the Linli graduates' preference for "fellow student" was a way of marking a narrower and more useful loyalty. The distinction runs through the rest of the chapter.

ch01.anchor: the great destruction and the massacre at Chungking
ch01.note: The demolitions and prison killings carried out in Chungking in late November 1949 as the Nationalists abandoned the city. Political prisoners at the Zhazidong and Baigongguan gaols were shot and the buildings fired; the dead numbered in the low hundreds. The Bath Cave named here, 渣滓洞, is Zhazidong itself -- a former coal pit whose name means "dross pit." These prisons stood in the compound the Sino-American Cooperative Organization had used, which is why the two are inseparable in Chinese memory; a later chapter of this book is devoted to that organization.

ch01.anchor: His own wife, whose name I withhold, was an underground Party member he had arrested; he raped her, took her by force as his wife, and made her publish a notice in the press renouncing the Party.
ch01.note: The book prints the man's surname followed by XX, redacting the rest, and gives the woman no name at all. Both redactions are the source's and are preserved. Published renunciations of Communist Party membership were a standard instrument of the Nationalist security services, extracted under duress and printed in the newspapers as evidence of the Party's collapse.

ch01.anchor: Mao Sen
ch01.note: Mao Sen (1908-1964), Juntong officer, head of the Shanghai garrison inspectorate and then of police and security in Shanghai before its fall in 1949; he directed the executions of political prisoners in the city's last months and went on to Taiwan, where he was shot dead in Japan in 1964 in circumstances never established. He is among the most notorious figures in this book's cast and is named here without elaboration.

ch01.anchor: After Hu Zongnan attacked Yan'an in 1947
ch01.note: Hu Zongnan's forces took Yan'an on 19 March 1947, after the Communist leadership had already evacuated it. The city was held for just over a year and recovered in April 1948. That the Juntong immediately installed an investigation office there, headed by a Linli graduate, is the detail Shen Zui wants: the occupation of an emptied town was still worth a secret-service establishment.

ch01.anchor: the Juntong selected to study in the United States just after the war against Japan ended
ch01.note: American training of Nationalist intelligence personnel followed directly from the wartime Sino-American Cooperative Organization, which had put US Navy instructors into Chinese secret-service training classes from 1943. The resentment Shen Zui records -- that two junior graduates were sent alongside departmental heads -- is a small measure of how valuable the American connection was thought to be.

ch01.anchor: are carrying on their evil work in Taiwan to this day
ch01.note: "To this day" means the early 1960s, when this chapter was written, not the 1995 or 2001 of publication. The book was composed in a period when the Nationalist government on Taiwan was an active adversary and its intelligence services were running operations against the mainland; the present tense here is a live one, and it is the tense in which the whole book's closing judgements are made.
